draft.title: Strong and sustainable growth
card: Economic growth is a rise in real GDP, which is the value of output with the effect of price changes removed. Real GDP is used so that a rise in prices alone is not mistaken for growth.
Strong growth is growth near the economy's long-run trend. For Australia this is about 3 per cent a year.
Sustainable growth is growth that can be kept up over time without causing problems such as rising inflation or damage to the environment.
Strong and sustainable growth raises output and incomes, and creates jobs. Over time this can lift living standards.
draft.remember: The goal is growth near trend that can be kept up, not the fastest growth possible.

a.q: Why is real GDP, not nominal GDP, used to judge economic growth?
opts: It removes the effect of price changes from output
It leaves out the output of the government sector
It counts only goods sold to other countries
It is measured more often than nominal GDP
a.why: Real GDP removes price changes, so a rise in it shows more output, not just higher prices. Nominal GDP can rise when prices rise even if output has not changed.
a.clue: Think about what happens to GDP if only prices go up.

b.q: Australia's real GDP grows by 3 per cent a year for several years, and inflation stays steady. Which description fits this growth best?
opts: Strong and sustainable, as it is near trend and can be kept up
Too fast, as any growth above zero strains the economy
Strong but not sustainable, as steady inflation is a problem
Weak, as growth must be well above 3 per cent to be strong
b.why: Growth of about 3 per cent is near the long-run trend, so it is strong. Steady inflation suggests it can be kept up, so it is also sustainable. Steady inflation is not a warning sign, so the growth is not unsustainable.
b.clue: Compare the growth rate with the long-run trend, then check for signs of strain.
